title: Streaming or De-Streaming in STEM Schools—Perspectives and Practices: A Multi-Case Study
content: Integrating engineering and technology into high school STEM pathways is vital for equipping students with the skills needed to succeed in modern industries and adapt to emerging technologies. This multi-case study examines how streaming and de-streaming practices in STEM high schools shape student and educator experiences in four Saudi educational directorates (Riyadh, Dammam, Al-Zulfi, and Arar). Through semi-structured interviews with students, teachers, and university professionals, the study explores perspectives on STEM pathways’ effectiveness and alignment with university and labor market needs. Results show that students’ pathway choices are driven primarily by personal interest and social influences, with limited impact from formal career interest tools. Students and teachers alike highlight the importance of teacher quality, resource availability, and career guidance, but also cite barriers such as inadequate training, insufficient resources, and unclear pathway structures. University professionals recognize the value of STEM pathways for readiness, but raise concerns about equity and sustainability. The study recommends a national STEM school model with integrated curricula, well-equipped facilities, ongoing teacher development, strengthened guidance, university-industry partnerships, and regular assessments to ensure continuous improvement and equitable outcomes. Ultimately, while teacher quality is crucial, achieving meaningful and continuous improvement requires comprehensive reforms throughout the educational system.
